message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; if you have a specific dispute, consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge a security deposit, but it cannot exceed **one month’s rent** for a month‑to‑month lease or **two months’ rent** for a fixed‑term lease.
• The deposit must be held in a **separate, interest‑bearing account** (unless the landlord is a bank).
• Within **30 days** after you move out, the landlord must return the deposit (or provide a written itemized list of deductions) | • Keep a copy of the lease and any receipt of the deposit.
• Inspect the unit before moving out and document any existing damage. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | • Texas law requires landlords to keep the premises in a **safe and habitable condition** (see Texas Property Code §92.001).
• Landlords must maintain plumbing, heating, electrical, and structural integrity. | • Report repairs in writing (email or text) and keep copies.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may withhold rent (in some cases) or repair and deduct, but check the lease first. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For month‑to‑month leases: **30‑day written notice** from either party to terminate.
• For fixed‑term leases: the lease term ends automatically unless you or the landlord gives notice. | • Provide notice in writing and keep a copy. | | **Rent Increases** | • Landlords may raise rent at the end of a lease term or with **30‑day written notice** for month‑to‑month. No statutory cap. | • Review the lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the **Texas Property Code §92.005**: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment, 30‑day notice for lease violation).
• After the notice period, the landlord files an **eviction lawsuit** (unlawful detainer). | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Attend court hearings; you can contest the eviction. | | **Privacy / Entry** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of all entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • Report any discriminatory actions to the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Lease Terms & Modifications** | • The lease is a binding contract. Both parties must honor its terms. | • If you want changes, negotiate in writing. | | **Utilities** | • The lease usually specifies who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities early. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • Many leases require landlord approval. | • Get written permission before subletting. | | **Legal Resources** | • **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** (https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection)
• **Texas Tenants Association** (https://www.texastenant.org)
• **Legal Aid of North Texas** (https://www.lanxtx.org) | • Use these sites for forms, guides, and attorney referrals. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the entire lease** – look for clauses on rent, deposits, maintenance, entry, and termination. 2. **Ask about the security deposit** – confirm the amount and the conditions for its return. 3. **Verify habitability** – ensure the unit meets basic health and safety standards. 4. **Check for hidden fees** – e.g., pet fees, parking, or “late fee” caps. 5. **Confirm utility responsibilities** – who pays what. 6. **Get everything in writing** – verbal agreements are hard to enforce. --- #### When Things Go Wrong | Issue | First Step | Next Step | |-------|------------|-----------| | Landlord refuses to return deposit | Send a written demand letter (include lease, deposit receipt, and a request for return). | If no response, file a small‑claims action (up to $20,000). | | Landlord fails to make repairs | Send a written notice of needed repairs. | If still ignored, you may withhold rent or repair and deduct (consult a lawyer). | | Unlawful eviction notice | Respond to the notice in writing. | File a defense in the unlawful detainer case. | | Discriminatory treatment | File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | Seek legal counsel for potential damages. | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, a fair security‑deposit process, reasonable notice for entry, and protection against unlawful eviction and discrimination. Keep records, communicate in writing, and use the resources above if you encounter problems.

There's no request for generating a contract. So we don't need to call the function. Just answer. Provide overview: security deposit, habitability, notice, eviction, etc. Also mention resources. Provide citations? Probably not needed. We'll give a concise but thorough answer.
